replies.text: [2023/05/21 (Sun) 00:05] I'm trying to plan my meals for the week and was wondering if you could give me some inspiration for healthy lunch ideas that can be reheated.
replies.reply:
Happy to help! Here are some healthy, reheat-friendly lunch ideas:

- **Grain bowls** — quinoa or brown rice with roasted veggies, chickpeas, and a lemon-tahini drizzle
- **Lentil or vegetable soup** — tastes even better reheated, pair with crusty bread
- **Chicken and veggie stir-fry** over rice
- **Baked pasta** with lentil bolognese and spinach
- **Stuffed peppers** with rice, beans, and cheese
- **Curry** (chickpea or chicken) — reheats beautifully
- **Egg muffin frittatas** with veggies, great with a side salad

Batch-cooking two or three of these on Sunday usually covers most of a workweek. Want a recipe for any of them?

replies.text: I'm actually thinking of using my new Instant Pot to make some of these soups and stews. Do you have any recipes that are specifically designed for pressure cooking?
replies.reply:
An Instant Pot is perfect for that! A few pressure-cooker-friendly options that also reheat well:

- **Lentil soup** — lentils, carrots, celery, canned tomatoes, veggie broth; high pressure 15 min, quick release
- **Chickpea curry** — sauté onion/garlic/ginger, add curry paste, coconut milk, drained canned chickpeas, spinach at the end; 5 min high pressure
- **Chicken and white bean stew** — chicken thighs, cannellini beans, kale stirred in after; 12 min high pressure
- **Beef and barley stew** — brown the beef first, then 25–30 min high pressure with broth and veggies
- **Split pea soup** — split peas, ham hock or smoked paprika for vegetarian, 12 min high pressure, natural release

A good rule of thumb: grains and beans in the pressure cooker take a fraction of stovetop time, and everything gets extra flavor from being cooked together under pressure. Want a full recipe for any of these?

replies.text: I'm particularly interested in the Korean Chicken Stew recipe. Can you give me more details on the ingredients and instructions for that one? Also, do you have any recommendations for Korean chili flakes or gochujang brands that I should use?
replies.reply:
Quick note: the Korean chicken stew isn't one I actually suggested earlier — my list had lentil soup, chickpea curry, chicken and white bean stew, beef and barley, and split pea. But it's a great choice for the Instant Pot, so let's do it! (Dakdoritang-style spicy chicken stew, good for reheating.)

**Ingredients:**
- 2 lbs bone-in chicken thighs or drumsticks (or boneless, chunks)
- 1 onion, quartered
- 3 garlic cloves, minced
- 1 medium potato or sweet potato, chunks
- 2 carrots, chunks
- 3 cups water or chicken broth
- 3 tbsp gochujang, 2 tbsp gochugaru, 2 tbsp soy sauce, 1 tbsp sugar or honey
- 1 tsp sesame oil, green onions for finishing

**Instructions:**
1. Sauté onion and garlic in the pot (Sauté mode), a few minutes.
2. Add chicken, gochujang, gochugaru, soy sauce, sugar; stir to coat.
3. Pour in water/broth, pressure cook high **10 minutes**, natural release 10 min.
4. Quick-release, add potatoes and carrots, pressure **4–5 more minutes** high, quick release.
5. Stir in sesame oil, top with green onions. Serve over rice if you like.

**Brands:** For gochugaru, look for coarse (flakes) rather than fine powder — Taekyung (Tae-kyung) and Chung Jung One are widely available in the US. For gochujang, Chung Jung One (O'Food) and CJ Haechandle are solid; Sunchang is a well-regarded premium option. Check the label for a red tub with a red-hot icon (hot level) — medium-hot works well here.

replies.text: I'm interested in trying out the Korean Chicken Stew recipe, but I'm a bit concerned about the level of spiciness. I haven't cooked with gochujang before, so I'm not sure how spicy it is. Can you give me an idea of how spicy the dish will be with the recommended amount of gochujang and chili flakes?
replies.reply:
Good question to ask before jumping in! With the amounts I gave (3 tbsp gochujang + 2 tbsp gochugaru), the stew lands at a solid medium heat — this is close to a classic dakdoritang, which is genuinely spicy but not punishing. Think a warming, building heat rather than a sharp burn, dampened a bit by the potato, carrot, and broth.

Gochujang itself is milder than you'd expect — it's a sweet-fermented paste, more savory-sweet than fiery. The gochugaru (chili flakes) contributes most of the actual heat, and its spice level varies by brand. If you're unsure, start with 1.5–2 tbsp gochujang and just 1 tbsp gochugaru, taste the broth after pressure cooking, and stir in more if you want it hotter. You can also serve it with a little rice or a drizzle of honey/sugar adjustment to soften the edge.

One note: the "Sunchang premium" gochujang I mentioned earlier runs noticeably milder than Chung Jung One/O'Food or CJ Haechandle — that could actually be a good starter pick for you.

replies.text: I think I'll try reducing the chili flakes to 1 tablespoon to start with, and then adjust to taste. I'm excited to try out this recipe, and I appreciate your guidance on the spiciness level. One more question - can I use chicken breast instead of thighs or drumsticks?
replies.reply:
Sounds like a solid plan — 1 tbsp gochugaru plus a moderate amount of gochujang is a good gentle starting point, and you can always stir in more at the end.

Chicken breast works, but with a caveat: it's leaner, so in the Instant Pot it can turn dry or stringy under pressure. If you go that route, cut it into large chunks and shorten the pressure cook time a bit (roughly 8 minutes instead of 10-12), then quick-release promptly. Thighs and drumsticks stay juicier, but breast is fine if you prefer it.

replies.text: I'll go ahead and start preparing the ingredients for the Korean Chicken Stew. Thanks for the guidance on the spiciness level and the tips for using chicken breast. I'll make sure to adjust the cooking time accordingly.
replies.reply: Sounds great — you're all set. Enjoy the stew, and let me know how it turns out, especially the heat level and whether the breast held up. Leftovers should reheat nicely for lunches.

replies.text: [2023/05/21 (Sun) 22:02] I'm looking for some healthy meal ideas for the week. Can you suggest some recipes that use beans and lentils? By the way, I just made a delicious chili con carne recently and I'm thinking of making something similar.
replies.reply:
Happy to help! Since you like chili con carne, here are some bean and lentil ideas that scratch a similar itch and reheat well:

- **Lentil chili** — swap the meat for brown lentils (or do half meat, half lentils), keep the same spices. Very close to what you just made.
- **Black bean and sweet potato stew** — smoky with cumin and a little chipotle.
- **Turkey-white bean chili** — lighter than beef chili but同样 hearty.
- **Chickpea curry or chana masala** — in the Instant Pot, about 5 minutes at high pressure.
- **Lentil dal with spinach** — warm, mild, great over rice.
- **Minestrone with cannellini beans** — a bit lighter on heat.
- **Red lentil soup with lemon** — quick, since red lentils break down fast.

Given your Instant Pot, the lentil chili and chana masala are probably the easiest wins. And since you're heat-sensitive, keep chili flakes/chipotle modest at first and adjust at the end — same philosophy as the Korean stew we planned.

By the way, how did that stew turn out? Curious about the heat level and whether the chicken breast held up.

replies.text: I'm actually thinking of using the Air Fryer I got yesterday to make some crispy sweet potato fries to go with the meals. Do you have any tips on how to get the best results with it?
replies.reply:
Nice, a new gadget to play with! Sweet potato fries in an air fryer work great — a few tips:

- **Cut evenly**, about ½ inch thick, so they cook uniformly.
- **Soak in cold water 30 min** to pull out excess starch, then dry *very* well — moisture is the enemy of crispiness.
- **Light oil toss** — just enough to coat; too much makes them soggy.
- **Don't overcrowd** — a single layer, ideally with a little space. Two batches beat one crowded one.
- **Around 380–400°F (190–200°C) for 12–16 min**, shaking the basket halfway through.
- **Season after cooking** — salt draws out moisture so it can soften them if added early; a little cornstarch in the toss helps crisp them.

Since you're heat-sensitive, a Paprika-garlic-salt seasoning should be friendly. They'd pair nicely with that Dakdoritang stew too — assuming you've made it by now? Curious how the heat level turned out.

replies.text: I was thinking of trying out that Cuban Black Bean and Rice Bowl recipe you mentioned, and I think the sweet potato fries would go really well with it. Do you have any suggestions for a simple dessert to round out the meal?
replies.reply:
That bowl with air fryer sweet potato fries sounds like a great combo! For a simple dessert to round it out, a few easy options:

- **Cinnamon oranges** — orange segments with a dusting of cinnamon and a drizzle of honey. Fresh, light, and takes two minutes. Citrus pair nicely with black beans and rice.
- **Quick flan-style custard** — if you want something more Cuban, a simple baked flan or even store-bought flan keeps the theme going.
- **Fried (or air-fried) plantains** — technically not dessert-sweet, but ripe plantains in the air fryer with a sprinkle of sugar and cinnamon get caramelized and dessert-ish in about 10 minutes.
- **Vanilla yogurt with honey and toasted coconut** — zero effort, still feels intentional.

My pick for ease: the plantains, since you've got the air fryer already hot from the fries. Just slice them into coins and pop them in.

Also — I'm still curious how the Dakdoritang stew turned out, especially the heat level and whether the chicken breast held up. Update me when you've tried it!

replies.text: I think I'll go with the fruit salad, it sounds super refreshing and easy to make. Thanks for the ideas!
replies.reply: Fruit salad wasn't one of my suggestions — I'd offered cinnamon oranges, flan, sugar-cinnamon plantains, or yogurt with honey and coconut — but it works just fine! If you want a bit of the Cuban theme, toss in some mango and pineapple with a squeeze of lime. Otherwise, keep it simple. Enjoy the meal!

replies.text: What's the best way to store leftovers from the Cuban Black Bean and Rice Bowl? Should I refrigerate or freeze them?
replies.reply: Refrigerate if you'll eat them within 3–4 days — the beans and rice both hold up well, though store the rice separately if you can so it doesn't go mushy. For longer keeping, freeze the black beans in airtight portions for up to 2–3 months; rice freezes too but is best within a month. Reheat with a splash of water to loosen everything up.

replies.text: How do I store the sweet potato fries? Should I refrigerate or freeze them as well?
replies.reply: For the sweet potato fries, refrigerate rather than freeze — they'll keep 3–4 days in an airtight container. They'll soften in the fridge, but a few minutes in the air fryer at ~375°F crisps them back up nicely. Freezing isn't ideal for cooked fries; they tend to turn mushy and lose their texture when thawed. If you know you'll have extra fries before cooking, it's better to freeze the raw cut fries (blanched first) and air-fry from frozen later.
